title: Malik ibn Anas
hookLine: the imam of Medina, who would not ride in the Prophet's city out of respect (reported)

lines: IN THE PROPHET'S CITY, HE WALKED.
cards: Fine horses stand tied outside a scholar's door in Medina. Gifts, he explains to a visiting student. The student asks the natural question: then why not ride one?
The answer, as his biographers tell it: he would be ashamed before Allah to tread with a hoof on ground where the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ lies buried. So in the Prophet's city, he walked.
The student is said to be a young al-Shafi'i, whom you'll meet properly soon. The man on foot founded the next school on this path. Today: Malik ibn Anas.

teach.b: Abu Hanifa was a man of Kufa, a busy city of merchants and debates. Malik was a man of Medina, where the Prophet lived, prayed, taught and was buried.
He was born there, taught there and, the reports say, rarely left except for pilgrimage. Hence the imam of Medina.

teach.h: WASHED AND PERFUMED TO TEACH HADITH.
teach.b: His biographers say that before teaching hadith he would wash, put on good clothes and perfume, and sit with dignity, because the words were the Prophet's.
A story people tell has a scorpion stinging him again and again during a lesson, and Malik not stopping until the hadith was finished.
Whether every detail is exact, the picture holds: he treated the Prophet's words like a guest of honor. Then his honesty.
A traveler is said to have come a long way with a list of questions, and Malik answered question after question with two words: la adri, I don't know. The man protested that he'd come so far.
Malik's reply, in the report: tell people that Malik doesn't know. For a jurist, I don't know was a form of respect too.
Last, a line attributed to him, pointing at the Prophet's grave: everyone's word can be taken or left, except the one in this grave. Some reports give versions of it to others.
Either way, it fits the man: careful with the Prophet's city, careful with his words, and careful with his own.

how: Maliki Muslims remember Imam Malik as the scholar of Medina who taught hadith with great reverence and was willing to say 'I don't know'; his school is followed in North and West Africa.

o: a Kufan judge who studied under Abu Hanifa
the imam of Medina who founded the Maliki school
the Companion who served the Prophet as a boy

games.q: Malik ibn Anas — tap the pairs.
p: gifts he would not ride in Medina
he washed and put on perfume

s: Malik would not ride in Medina, his biographers report, out of respect for the Prophet's grave
he was ashamed, he said, to tread with a hoof on that ground.
a great jurist never answers I don't know
Malik is remembered for answering a traveler's questions with la adri, I don't know.
Malik was a scholar of Kufa
Abu Hanifa was of Kufa; Malik was the imam of Medina.

games.q: a traveler has come a long way with a list of questions. you don't know the answer to several. what do you do?
o: give your best guess so his trip isn't wasted.
send him to someone else without a word.
say I don't know, and let him tell people so.
games.why: in the report, Malik says la adri, I don't know, and tells the man to let people know that Malik doesn't know.

practice: If you can, stand and walk a few slow steps around your room; if not, walk in your mind into a place that deserves care, a grave you've visited, a house of worship, your grandmother's kitchen.

Notice your feet, your pace, your voice getting lower, what you'd touch and what you wouldn't, then stand still for a moment. If you pray, you can greet that place with a greeting your tradition uses.

wordCard.voice: Malik ibn Anas. The imam of Medina, founder of the Maliki school, remembered for his respect for the Prophet's city and words, and for saying I don't know. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: I don't know; the words Malik is remembered for using without embarrassment.

carryVoice: Your line: the imam of medina. For him, I don't know was a kind of respect. Go gently.

sources.ref: Biographical reports on Malik (e.g. Qadi 'Iyad, Tartib al-Madarik)
